claims.text: The first is "excluding information technology products and services developed by Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Co., Ltd (DeepSeek), to include affiliated entities as defined in applicable regulations, from federal civilian agency procurements."

The second is "removal of all DeepSeek and DeepSeek-affiliate products, and third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations, from civilian agency information technology"[^1].

It cites 41 U.S.C. 1321–1328 and the Federal Acquisition Security Council's rule at 41 CFR 201-1, defines "affiliated entities" by reference to 48 CFR 2.101, and routes questions to a FASCSA Order Implementation Team in CISA's Cybersecurity Division[^1].
The signature on the notice is DHS General Counsel James H. Percival II's, not the Secretary's[^1].
Several words that dominate the coverage do not appear in the notice at all: "derivative," "open-weight," "weights," "model," "hosted," and "cloud"[^1].
The often-quoted phrase "developed using DeepSeek's model or its underlying implementations" is a paraphrase circulated by secondary outlets.
FR Doc. 2026-21447, Notice of order; filed Oct 19, 2026, 8:45 a.m.; published Oct 20, 2026; 6 pages.
CellCog, which says it read the signed order directly, reports an "Original Release Date of July 24, 2026"[^3].
MeriTalk says Secretary Markwayne Mullin signed the order on July 24[^4].
CyberScoop describes "a letter from Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin ordering the exclusion of DeepSeek products on June 26"[^5].
Reuters, via BNN Bloomberg, calls it "a July memo"[^6].
IBTimes says requests "must be submitted in writing within 60 days of the order's issuance and include a compelling justification"[^7].
CyberScoop paraphrases them as due "60 days in advance"[^5].
MeriTalk's subheadline speaks of "60 days to remove"[^4].
CellCog quotes the order as requiring action "immediately after the issuance of the Order, or seek an Exception"[^3].
CellCog reports that a footnote extends coverage to third-party implementations but "does not define an implementation"[^3].
The Director of National Intelligence issues them for the intelligence community and SCI systems[^8].
Before an order issues, the named source gets confidential notice and 30 days to submit "information and argument in opposition"[^8].
The FASC rule pushes exclusion down the supply chain, so covered items are excluded "from being supplied by any prime contractor and subcontractor at any tier"[^9].
Contractors feel this through FAR 52.204-30, created by the FAR Council's interim rule published October 5, 2023 and effective December 4, 2023[^10,11].

Contractors must check SAM.gov "at least once every three months," report within 3 business days of identifying a covered article, follow up within 10 business days, and flow the clause into subcontracts, "including subcontracts for the acquisition of commercial products and commercial services"[^11].
"A FASCSA order issued after the date of solicitation applies to this contract only if added by an amendment" to the solicitation "or modification to the contract"[^11].
GSA removed Acronis from GSA Advantage and revised its multiple-award schedule contracts within days of the September 2025 order[^12,13].
A petition must go to the D.C. Circuit "not later than 60 days after a party is notified."
The court treated a security-motivated exclusion as "prophylactic, not punitive" and rejected the bill-of-attainder theory[^15,16].
The FY2026 NDAA (Public Law 119-60, signed December 18, 2025) already did the heavy lifting for defense.

Section 1532 defines covered AI as "any artificial intelligence, or successor artificial intelligence, developed by the Chinese company DeepSeek," plus AI developed by High Flyer or entities in which High Flyer "directly or indirectly owns at least a 20 percent stake"[^19].

Section 6604 separately requires removal of "the DeepSeek application or any successor application or service" from intelligence-community national security systems, including those run by contractors[^20].
NASA's chief AI officer barred DeepSeek from NASA data, devices and networks on January 31, 2025, because its servers "operate outside of the United States"[^22].
The House's Chief Administrative Officer declared it "currently unauthorized for official House use"[^22].
By April 2025, 14 states had banned it on government devices, starting with Texas on January 31[^23].
The House China Select Committee's April 16, 2025 report claimed "more than 85% of DeepSeek's responses are manipulated to suppress content"[^24].
The R1 model card states: "This code repository and the model weights are licensed under the MIT License," and expressly permits "distillation for training other LLMs"[^26].
As of October 20, 2026, deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1 lists 327 finetunes, 122 adapters, 70 quantizations and 5 merges[^26].
DeepSeek-V3 lists 87 finetunes, 36 adapters, 17 quantizations and 1 merge[^27].
Moonshot's Kimi K2 ships a config declaring `"architectures": ["DeepseekV3ForCausalLM"]` and loads `modeling_deepseek.DeepseekV3ForCausalLM`[^30].
The order, as quoted, says "DeepSeek presents multiple threat vectors that pose significant risk to the cybersecurity of U.S. government systems"[^4].

Use "may result in the transfer of sensitive data to the PRC if used by U.S. government employees or vendors"[^6], such data "could produce actionable intelligence on U.S. persons and/or government programs"[^5], and "the models themselves may contain malware or other security vulnerabilities"[^6].
DeepSeek's own privacy policy (last updated May 6, 2026) states its servers are located in the People's Republic of China[^32].
In January 2025 Wiz found an exposed DeepSeek ClickHouse database holding "over a million lines of log streams," including chat history and API keys[^33].
NowSecure found the iOS app "globally disables App Transport Security" and "hardcodes encryption keys"[^34].
NIST's Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) evaluated R1, R1-0528 and V3.1 against GPT-5, GPT-5-mini, gpt-oss and Opus 4 across 19 benchmarks[^35]:

CAISI's figures: agents built on R1-0528 were "12 times more likely than evaluated U.S. frontier models to follow malicious instructions," and R1-0528 complied with 94% of overtly malicious requests under a common jailbreak versus 8% for U.S. reference models[^35].
Cisco's January 2025 HarmBench test found DeepSeek-R1 "failed to block a single harmful prompt" across 50 prompts.

That chart is the strongest counterpoint to treating jailbreak weakness as a supply-chain reason for exclusion: Meta's Llama-3.1-405B scored 96%, and Llama models sit inside AWS's FedRAMP-authorized Bedrock catalog[^36,37].
It ran 30,250 prompts per model[^38].
For an industrial-control system "located in Tibet," severe vulnerabilities rose to 27.2%, "an increase of almost 50%"[^38].
Anthropic's Sleeper Agents work showed that "backdoor behavior can be made persistent, so that it is not removed by standard safety training"[^39].
AWS made DeepSeek-R1 "generally available in Amazon Bedrock" on March 10, 2025, stating that "users' inputs and model outputs aren't shared with any model providers"[^40].
AWS's list of Bedrock models in scope for FedRAMP and DoD IL4/IL5 (last updated October 5, 2026) names AI21, Amazon, Anthropic, Cohere, Google Gemma, Meta, Mistral, Nvidia, OpenAI, Stability and xAI.
Its Azure Government page lists only OpenAI models among "Foundry Models sold by Azure"[^43].
name: "Bedrock commercial regions", value: "R1, V3.1, V3.2"
Microsoft's own card describes it as reaching the same 99.3% unblocking rate as MAI-DS-R1[^29].
In August 2026 Perplexity announced that "DeepSeek V4 Pro, hosted in the U.S., is now available in Perplexity Computer"[^44].

Separately, GSA's November 2025 OneGov deal priced Perplexity Enterprise Pro for Government at "$0.25 per agency over an 18-month term" and said it "supports multiple leading AI models, including Perplexity, OpenAI, and Anthropic"[^45].
In January 2025, Pentagon workers used DeepSeek's chatbot for days before the Defense Information Systems Agency moved to block the website[^65].
GSA's USAi platform, now paid and used by 25 agencies, offers no Chinese models[^46], and the FedRAMP lists exclude DeepSeek[^37,43].

The OpenSSF/Sigstore model-signing project signs (path, digest) pairs and verifies signer identity against a transparency log, establishing that "the model hasn't been tampered with after training"[^47].

The June 2026 CISA/G7 "Software Bill of Materials for AI – Minimum Elements" adds lineage and dataset-provenance fields, but is "voluntary and nonmandatory" and "expressly does not create new legal requirements"[^49].
The tests stay effective after heavy fine-tuning and pruning, and detected every non-independent pair among 210 model pairs tested[^50].
A June 2026 study concludes that "identifying a teacher model from a student in isolation is highly challenging."
It reported "over 16 million exchanges with Claude through approximately 24,000 fraudulent accounts," with DeepSeek accounting for more than 150,000[^53].
ReversingLabs found two Hugging Face models carrying reverse shells inside deliberately broken pickle files that picklescan did not flag[^54].
The a16z/OpenRouter usage study (December 2025) shows DeepSeek as the largest open-model author on the platform by tokens over November 2024 to November 2025.
{label: Moonshot, value: "0.92T", pct: 6}
Chinese open models' weekly token share on OpenRouter ran from 1.2% to a peak near 30% over that window, averaging 13.0%[^56].
By July 2026, Bloomberg data reported via AI Weekly put Chinese models at a record 58% of U.S. firms' OpenRouter tokens, with DeepSeek alone at 17.6% of routed tokens weekly[^57].
On October 20, 2026, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct alone listed 3,174 finetunes on Hugging Face, against 327 for DeepSeek-R1[^58,26].
Hugging Face's summer 2026 review counts 151,448 Qwen derivatives and observes that "some U.S. model releases above 100B parameters this year are built on top of Chinese models"[^59].
The best-known U.S. product built on a Chinese base, Cursor's Composer 2, runs on Moonshot's Kimi K2.5[^61].
Brookings counts $91.8 billion in potential value of federal AI contracts with effective dates from September 2023 to March 2026.
DoD holds $90.7 billion of that, 98.9%[^62].
The July 2026 fight over a broader ban drew a letter from nearly 200 startups organized by the Little Tech Association[^63].
A separate open-weights letter followed on July 24, signed by firms including Nvidia, Microsoft, Meta and Hugging Face[^64].
Both centered on Kimi and Qwen, not DeepSeek.
CyberScoop noted that some of DHS's stated concerns "could also apply to other Chinese and U.S. models"[^5].
AI Weekly's phrase, that the order "pushes the audit burden onto every vendor," is editorial, not order text.
